title: Does AI Help Junior or Senior Developers More?
question: Does AI help junior or senior developers more?
alternates: Who Really Gets the AI Productivity Boost?
The Experience Paradox in AI Coding Studies
premise: The 'far more for experts' claim is not supported: Microsoft's field experiment (short-tenure 27-39% versus long-tenure 8-13%, mostly not significant), Shan's RCT, Peng's Copilot trial and the code-ownership experiment all found gains concentrated among less experienced developers, and METR found experienced maintainers slowed, more so on tasks they knew well. The Google trial is the exception: on code unfamiliar to everyone, seniors gained if anything more, not significantly. That pattern is the resolution: gains concentrate where the developer lacks context, which juniors usually do and seniors do on unfamiliar code. Skill in using the tools matters (habitual AI users' code scored better downstream in the Echoes trial) but the evidence for a steep skill curve is thin and partly self-reported, and METR saw no improvement over the first 50 hours.
whyWatch: Influencers say AI is a multiplier for experts. Most trials found the opposite, one found a hint the other way, and the reason they differ says something about when the tools help anyone.
tension: 'Amplifies experts far more' against trials where juniors and short-tenure developers gained most and experienced maintainers were slowed.

arc.hook: Two engineers, one senior, one junior, both switch on the same tool. The influencers say the senior pulls ahead. The trials say otherwise.
arc.conflict: Five trials point one way, Google's points the other, and 'far more' for experts has no support anywhere.
arc.evidence: Microsoft/Accenture by tenure, Shan's moderation analysis, Peng's heterogeneity, the code-ownership experiment, METR's slowdown by task familiarity, and Google's unfamiliar-code design.
arc.resolution: The tools help most where the developer has the least context. Juniors have less of it everywhere; seniors have less of it on unfamiliar code. Using the tools well is a skill, but not yet a measured steep one.
arc.takeaway: Point the tools at unfamiliar work, expect less on code you know by heart, and treat '10x for experts' as marketing.

central.text: The evidence does not support "AI coding tools amplify experienced engineers far more than novices"

claims.text: AI coding tools amplify experienced engineers far more than novices

guess.note: Experts get more reliable results and catch errors, but several RCTs show larger measured speedups for juniors, and METR found experts slowed; contested.

questions.question: Does AI help junior or senior developers more?

central.text: The evidence does not support "AI coding tools amplify experienced engineers far more than novices"

questions.premise: The 'far more for experts' claim is not supported: Microsoft's field experiment (short-tenure 27-39% versus long-tenure 8-13%, mostly not significant), Shan's RCT, Peng's Copilot trial and the code-ownership experiment all found gains concentrated among less experienced developers, and METR found experienced maintainers slowed, more so on tasks they knew well. The Google trial is the exception: on code unfamiliar to everyone, seniors gained if anything more, not significantly. That pattern is the resolution: gains concentrate where the developer lacks context, which juniors usually do and seniors do on unfamiliar code. Skill in using the tools matters (habitual AI users' code scored better downstream in the Echoes trial) but the evidence for a steep skill curve is thin and partly self-reported, and METR saw no improvement over the first 50 hours.
questions.tension: 'Amplifies experts far more' against trials where juniors and short-tenure developers gained most and experienced maintainers were slowed.
questions.whyWatch: Influencers say AI is a multiplier for experts. Most trials found the opposite, one found a hint the other way, and the reason they differ says something about when the tools help anyone.

arc.hook: Two engineers, one senior, one junior, both switch on the same tool. The influencers say the senior pulls ahead. The trials say otherwise.
arc.conflict: Five trials point one way, Google's points the other, and 'far more' for experts has no support anywhere.
arc.evidence: Microsoft/Accenture by tenure, Shan's moderation analysis, Peng's heterogeneity, the code-ownership experiment, METR's slowdown by task familiarity, and Google's unfamiliar-code design.
arc.resolution: The tools help most where the developer has the least context. Juniors have less of it everywhere; seniors have less of it on unfamiliar code. Using the tools well is a skill, but not yet a measured steep one.
arc.takeaway: Point the tools at unfamiliar work, expect less on code you know by heart, and treat '10x for experts' as marketing.

questions.question: Why can AI assistance cost expert programmers more time than it saves?

central.text: AI assistance must be very reliable to save experts time, because checking and fixing its output is costly

questions.premise: METR's developers accepted under 44% of Cursor generations and lost significant time reviewing, testing and modifying output before rejecting it; low reliability is one of the listed causes of the 19% slowdown. Google's migration report describes throttling change generation so that reviewers could keep up, and the vibe-coding review names the 'verification gap' as its central synthesis. Anthropic's engineers skip the tool for short or context-heavy tasks and describe a paradox of supervision: checking needs the skills overuse may erode. Limits: the acceptance figure is from 16 developers with early-2025 tools; the bottleneck evidence is a company report and a review of reports; the skill claims are qualitative.
questions.tension: Generation got cheap; checking did not, and for people who could have written it themselves the check costs more than the typing saved.
questions.whyWatch: The slowdown result is famous; the mechanism is less known and more useful: experts accepted under half of the suggestions and paid for the rest in review.

arc.hook: A suggestion appears in the editor. For an expert, the cheapest move is often to delete it. Why?
arc.conflict: The tool saved typing; it created checking, and checking is the expensive part for someone who already knows the answer.
arc.evidence: METR's acceptance rate and review time; Google throttling generation to review capacity; the verification gap; Anthropic's supervision paradox.
arc.resolution: AI help pays when the check is cheaper than the work it replaces; for experts on familiar code it often is not, and the skill to check cannot be outsourced.
arc.takeaway: Measure your acceptance rate; if you delete most of what the tool writes, use it for the work you cannot already do.
